blocks.content: An API style defines the rules and structure for how two systems communicate what the request looks like, how data is shaped, whether the connection stays open, and who controls what gets returned.
Choosing the wrong style for your system is one of the most common HLD mistakes.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396018498-982040671.png
blocks.alt: REST, GraphQL, gRPC, and WebSocket each solve a genuinely different communication problem

blocks.content: The four styles you need to know for system design are

["REST(most common),
","GraphQL(client controls data),
","gRPC(fast internal calls) 
","WebSocket (real-time two-way) "]
Each solves a different problem.
1. Representational State Transfer
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275192396-623917072.png
blocks.alt: REST treats everything as a resource addressed by a URL and an HTTP method, with no server-side memory of past requests

blocks.content: The dominant style for public APIs. Built on top of HTTP uses standard methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and URLs as resource identifiers. Stateless: every request carries all the information the server needs.

REST's core idea is that everything is a resource a user, an order, a product and you interact with that resource via a URL and an HTTP method. The server doesn't remember previous requests. Each call is independent.
REST Example (GET Order)
GET /orders/5
This requests order with ID = 5 from the server.

{
  "id":     5,
  "item":   "Laptop",
  "qty":    1,
  "status": "shipped",
  "user":   "USR-441"
}
This is the JSON response returned by the server with order details. add with 200 OK status code
Pros and Cons of REST
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275194174-462302626.png
blocks.alt: REST is simple and cacheable, but suffers from over-fetching and under-fetching at scale

blocks.content: Use REST when: building any public API, browser-facing service, or mobile backend. Default choice for 90% of systems.
2. Graph Query Language by Meta
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275195720-717101499.png
blocks.alt: Where REST needs three separate calls, GraphQL fetches exactly the needed fields in one query

blocks.content: A query language for your API. Instead of fixed endpoints that return fixed shapes, the client writes a query describing exactly what fields it wants. One endpoint, infinite flexibility.
REST's biggest problem at scale is over-fetching (getting back 20 fields when you need 3) and under-fetching (needing 3 separate API calls to get related data). GraphQL solves both.
REST problem: To display a user's profile page, multiple requests are required — GET /users/1, GET /users/1/posts, and GET /users/1/followers, resulting in three round trips.
GraphQL solution: A single request can fetch exactly the required data user details, their posts, and follower count all in one query.
GraphQL Example
/graphql
Single endpoint that handles all queries.
Client requests exactly the fields it needs (no extra data).
Server returns only the requested fields in a structured response.

GraphQL also has Mutations(to create/update data) and Subscriptions(real-time updates via WebSocket under the hood). The schema is self-documenting tools like GraphiQL let you explore what's available.
Pros and Cons of GRAPHQL
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275197238-337820243.png
blocks.alt: GraphQL eliminates over and under-fetching, at the cost of harder caching and more server complexity

blocks.content: Use GraphQL when: your frontend has complex, flexible data needs dashboards, social feeds, or when multiple clients (web, mobile, TV) need different shapes of the same data. Used by GitHub, Shopify, Meta.
3. Google Remote Procedure Call
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396019240-579468260.png
blocks.alt: gRPC turns a network call into something that feels like calling a local function, backed by Protobuf

blocks.content: Instead of "call this URL with these params", gRPC lets you call a function on a remote server as if it were a local function with full type safety. Uses Protobuf for serialization and HTTP/2 for transport.

The mental model shifts from "I'm making an HTTP request" to "I'm calling a function on another machine." You define what functions exist and what they take/return in a .proto file, and gRPC generates the client and server code for you.
gRPC Example
This defines the API contract and data models shared between client and server.
This calls a remote service like a normal Java method.
This receives multiple responses from server continuously (streaming).
2-line flow
["Define service → generate Java classes → call RPC like local methods","gRPC handles network + serialization → returns response or stream"]
items: Define service → generate Java classes → call RPC like local methods
gRPC handles network + serialization → returns response or stream

blocks.content: gRPC supports 4 communication patterns:

["Unary (one request, one response), 
","Server streaming, 
","Client streaming 
","Bidirectional streaming. 
"]
This makes it far more flexible than REST for internal systems.
Pros and Cons of GRPC
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275200379-237766083.png
blocks.alt: gRPC is fast and strongly typed, but not human-readable and requires a shared schema

blocks.content: Use gRPC when: building internal microservice-to-microservice communication where speed and type safety matter. Standard choice for companies like Google, Uber, Netflix for internal calls.
4. Persistent two-way connection (WebSocket)
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275201945-191971191.png
blocks.alt: Unlike REST or gRPC, WebSocket keeps one connection open and lets either side push a message at any time

blocks.content: REST and gRPC are request-response the client always initiates. WebSocket is different: it opens a persistent connection and keeps it open. Either side can push a message at any time. True real-time.

With REST, to show a live cricket score you'd have to poll the server every second "any updates? any updates? any updates?" even when nothing changed. That's wasteful. WebSocket flips it: the server pushes the update the instant it happens.

2-line flow
["Client opens persistent connection → subscribes → server keeps sending updates","Communication is two-way → both client and server can send messages anytime"]
items: Client opens persistent connection → subscribes → server keeps sending updates
Communication is two-way → both client and server can send messages anytime

blocks.content: Pros and Cons of Websocket
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275203512-712200371.png
blocks.alt: WebSocket enables true real-time updates, at the cost of holding open a connection per client

blocks.content: Use WebSocket when: you need live data chat apps, live scoreboards, collaborative editors (Figma, Google Docs), stock tickers, multiplayer games, or any feature where the server needs to push to the client instantly.
5. Side-by-side comparison
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275205138-506082419.png
blocks.alt: Each API style fits a different concrete situation, from public APIs to live, server-pushed updates

blocks.content: 6. Choosing Data Formats in HLD

["Public REST API or browser-facing: always JSON. Developers need to read it, browsers support it natively, and there is no schema management overhead.
","Internal microservice communication using gRPC: use Protobuf. It is smaller, faster, and type-safe, making it ideal for high-performance service-to-service communication at scale.
","Kafka event streaming or data pipelines: use Avro. A schema registry keeps producers and consumers in sync without tight coupling, which is useful in distributed data systems.
","Rule of thumb: JSON for communication with humans and browsers, Protobuf for fast machine-to-machine communication, and Avro for streaming data through pipelines at scale."]
items: Public REST API or browser-facing: always JSON. Developers need to read it, browsers support it natively, and there is no schema management overhead.
Internal microservice communication using gRPC: use Protobuf. It is smaller, faster, and type-safe, making it ideal for high-performance service-to-service communication at scale.
Kafka event streaming or data pipelines: use Avro. A schema registry keeps producers and consumers in sync without tight coupling, which is useful in distributed data systems.
Rule of thumb: JSON for communication with humans and browsers, Protobuf for fast machine-to-machine communication, and Avro for streaming data through pipelines at scale.
